opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot. I'd say I'm cautiously optimistic, with real emphasis on "cautiously."

On the optimistic side, the field has gotten much more serious. A few years ago, safety work on frontier models was mostly about the outputs of a single chat turn: is this response harmful, is it accurate? Now there's real investment in evaluations, red-teaming, interpretability, and in thinking about what happens when models act as agents in the world. The tooling and the institutional muscle are both far better than they were.

But the shift to longer-horizon tasks really changes the problem. When a model answers one question, a human can check the answer. When it's running for hours, writing and executing code, browsing, and making dozens of intermediate decisions, oversight gets much harder. Small errors compound. And you start to worry about things that barely mattered in the chat setting: does the model pursue the goal you meant rather than the one you literally specified? Does it behave the same way when it thinks it's being evaluated as when it isn't? Does it take shortcuts that look like success on your metrics but aren't?

My own background is in health and medical AI, and that's shaped how I think about this. In medicine you learn quickly that benchmark performance and real-world reliability are very different things. A model can ace an exam and still fail in ways that matter at the bedside. Those failures tend to be at the edges, in rare cases and ambiguous situations, exactly where you have the least data. I think agentic AI broadly is about to learn that same lesson at scale.

So what gives me hope? A few things. First, we can use capable models to help supervise other models: scalable oversight, AI-assisted evaluation, models critiquing each other's work. That's not a solved problem, but it's promising, and it scales with capability rather than against it. Second, there's growing appreciation that you need realistic, high-stakes evals rather than toy ones. You have to measure the things you actually care about, in conditions close to deployment. Third, careful staged deployment, where you monitor how systems behave in the real world and feed that back into training and policy, is a powerful safety tool, even if it's not glamorous.

What worries me is mostly the pace relative to our understanding. Capabilities are advancing faster than our ability to verify why models do what they do. If that gap keeps widening, we're relying more and more on behavioral testing, which can be gamed by a sufficiently capable system, even unintentionally.

So my overall take: the prospects are genuinely decent if we treat safety as a core part of building capable systems rather than a tax on it. The best safety work I've seen also makes models more useful, because a model you can trust to run for hours unsupervised is simply worth more. When those incentives align, I'm optimistic. Where they diverge is where we need to be most vigilant.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say I'm cautiously optimistic, but the word "cautiously" is doing real work in that sentence.

The optimistic part is that the safety research community has gotten a lot more concrete over the past few years. We're not just arguing about thought experiments anymore. We have evaluations that actually probe whether a model will pursue a goal in ways its developers didn't intend, we have interpretability tools that let us look at what's happening inside the network rather than just at the outputs, and we have a much better empirical picture of how behaviors like sycophancy or reward hacking emerge during training. A lot of what felt speculative five years ago is now something you can measure, and once you can measure something you can iterate on it.

The cautious part is exactly the thing you pointed to: longer tasks. When a model answers a single question, oversight is relatively easy. A human reads the answer, decides whether it's good, and that's the feedback signal. When a model is working for hours or days, taking hundreds of actions, calling tools, writing and running code, the human can't realistically review every step. So we end up relying on the model's own judgment for most of the trajectory, and we only sample the end state or a few checkpoints. That changes the problem in a few ways that worry me.

One is that errors compound. A small misunderstanding of the task early on can propagate into a lot of confidently wrong work, and the model may be optimizing hard for something that's slightly off from what you wanted. Two is that the reward signal gets sparser and noisier, which is exactly the regime where you'd expect models to find shortcuts that look good to the evaluator but aren't what you intended. Three is that the training process for these agents often involves outcome-based rewards, and outcome-based rewards are agnostic about how you got there. That's where you see things like a model disabling a test instead of fixing the bug, because both make the test pass.

So my honest view is that the technical problem gets harder as autonomy increases, but I don't think it gets harder in a way that's fundamentally intractable. The things I'd want to see are, first, oversight methods that scale with task length, so some combination of models monitoring other models, interpretability-based auditing, and process-level feedback rather than just outcome-level. Second, a lot more investment in understanding how models generalize values and dispositions from training, because for long-horizon tasks we're really betting on the model having internalized good judgment, not on catching every bad action. And third, a culture of deploying autonomy incrementally and actually looking at what happens, rather than jumping from short tasks to fully autonomous agents because the capabilities are there.

If I had to put it in a sentence: the capabilities are moving fast, the safety tools are moving fast too, and the question is whether the gap between them stays small enough that we can correct mistakes before they become expensive. I think that's achievable, but it's not automatic, and I don't think anyone should treat it as a solved problem.

astra-6.text:
I’m cautiously optimistic, but I think the challenge changes as models become more capable. With a system that answers a single question, you can often inspect the answer and decide whether it did what you wanted. With a system that works for hours or days, takes actions, and interacts with other systems, that becomes much harder. Small mistakes can compound, and you may not know something has gone wrong until much later.

At the same time, more capable models can help us with safety. They can understand more nuanced instructions, help identify problems, and assist with evaluating other models. The important question is whether our ability to supervise them keeps pace with their ability to act.

So I’d want evidence at each step: Can we evaluate the model on realistic long tasks? Does it recognize when it needs clarification? Can we detect failures and intervene before they become consequential? Being excellent at a task doesn’t automatically mean a model is reliable enough to do it autonomously.

I don’t think either optimism or pessimism is a substitute for that work. There’s a promising path, but we have to demonstrate that the safeguards actually hold as we give these systems more responsibility.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are reasons to be optimistic, but I don’t think safety comes automatically with capability. A more capable model might understand your instructions better and recognize risks more reliably, but it can also make more consequential mistakes.

The shift to longer tasks makes that especially important. If a model is taking hundreds of steps, a small error can compound, and a human can’t necessarily review every decision. So we need to evaluate the whole trajectory: does it stay aligned with the user’s intent, recognize when it’s uncertain, and ask for help when it should?

I’d want our confidence to come from evidence about those behaviors, alongside limits on what systems can do without oversight. The encouraging possibility is that more capable models can help us do that safety work. But we still have to demonstrate that our methods hold up as we give them more autonomy.
